description: ArchiMate 3.2 modeling language: framework, element and relationship notation (image cards in both directions), layer metamodels, viewpoints and derivation rules. For enterprise architects modeling at work or preparing for ArchiMate Foundation/Practitioner.

notes.front: What is the ArchiMate language for?
notes.back: An open modeling language (The Open Group) with uniform concepts and notation to describe, analyse and visualise enterprise architecture across business domains, unambiguously.
notes.extra: Covers processes, organisation, information flows, applications and infrastructure, and the dependencies between them.

notes.back: A 3×3 grid: layers Business, Application, Technology × aspects Passive Structure, Behavior, Active Structure.

notes.front: What does the ArchiMate Full Framework add to the Core Framework?
notes.back: Layers Strategy, Physical and Implementation & Migration, plus the Motivation aspect that crosses all layers.

notes.front: ArchiMate top-level concept hierarchy: what does Concept specialise into, and what does Element specialise into?
notes.back:
Concept → Element, Relationship, Relationship Connector.
Element → Structure, Behavior, Motivation, Composite element.
The generic term for either an element or a relationship.
Elements that perform behavior: the subjects of activity (actors, roles, components, nodes).
notes.analogy: Grammar: active structure is the subject, behavior the verb, passive structure the object ("the clerk handles the claim").
notes.extra: Aspects classify elements independently of layer.

notes.back: What happens: processes, functions, interactions, events and services performed by active structure elements.
Objects on which behavior is performed: usually information/data objects, but also physical material.

notes.front: Which ArchiMate abstraction lets you model what happens without saying who does it?
notes.back: Behavior vs active structure: behavior elements can be modeled before (or without) assigning a performer.

notes.front: ArchiMate's conceptual → logical → physical chain for information: which elements, linked how?
notes.back: Business object → data object → artifact, each realized by the next via realization.
notes.extra: Example: 'Customer file' ← 'Customer record' ← customers.db.

notes.back: External (services, interfaces) expose functionality to the environment and hide implementation. Internal (processes, functions, components, actors) realize it.

notes.front: Why does ArchiMate define concepts separately from their notation?
notes.back: So the meaning stays fixed while tools may offer alternative notations for different audiences. The standard notation still aids recognisability.

notes.front: In ArchiMate, what does nesting one element inside another mean?
notes.back: An alternative notation for a relationship, allowed for composition, aggregation, assignment (and grouping). The relationship still exists in the model.
notes.extra: Pitfall: nesting is ambiguous about which of these relationships is meant; the model must say.

notes.text: ArchiMate conventional layer colours (not normative): Business = {{c1::yellow}}, Application = {{c2::blue}}, Technology/Physical = {{c3::green}}, Strategy = {{c4::tan/orange}}, Motivation = {{c5::purple}}, Implementation & Migration = {{c6::pink}}.
ArchiMate corner shapes (normative cues): {{c1::square}} corners = structure elements, {{c2::rounded}} corners = behavior elements, {{c3::cut (diagonal)}} corners = motivation elements.

notes.front: In ArchiMate, what is a composite element? Give examples.
notes.back: An element that consists of other concepts, possibly from several aspects or layers: Grouping, Location, Product, Plateau.

notes.front: ArchiMate generic metamodel: how do internal active structure, internal behavior, service and interface connect?
notes.back: Active structure assigned to internal behavior; behavior realizes a service; active structure composes an interface, which is assigned to the service.
notes.extra: Behavior accesses passive structure; events trigger behavior.

notes.back: An element that aggregates or composes concepts that belong together based on some common characteristic.
notes.extra:
Layer: Composite (layer-independent)

Aspect: Composite

Dashed rectangle with a tab; can group any concepts, including relationships between groupings. Aggregation (default) or composition semantics.

notes.back: A place or position where structure elements can be located or behavior can be performed.
notes.extra:
Layer: Composite (layer-independent)

Aspect: Composite

Typically connected with an aggregation relationship (or assignment) to the located elements.

notes.front: How does service orientation link the ArchiMate core layers?
notes.back: Each layer offers services to the layer above (Technology → Application → Business → customers), linked by serving; lower-layer elements realize more abstract ones above.
notes.analogy: A restaurant: the kitchen (technology) serves the waiters (applications), who serve the guests (business).

notes.text: ArchiMate relationship categories: {{c1::structural}} (composition, aggregation, assignment, realization) · {{c2::dependency}} (serving, access, influence, association) · {{c3::dynamic}} (triggering, flow) · {{c4::other}} (specialization). Connector: {{c5::junction}}.

notes.back: Represents that an element consists of one or more other concepts — a whole-part relationship where the part can belong to only one whole and cannot exist independently of it.
notes.extra:
Line style: solid line

Filled diamond at the end of the WHOLE (composer). Nesting is an alternative notation.

notes.back: Represents that an element combines one or more other concepts — a whole-part relationship where the part may belong to multiple wholes and can exist independently.
notes.extra:
Line style: solid line

Open (hollow) diamond at the end of the whole. Nesting is an alternative notation.

notes.back: Represents the allocation of responsibility, performance of behavior, storage, or execution — e.g., a business role assigned to a business process, an application component assigned to an application function, an artifact deployed on a node.
notes.extra:
Line style: solid line

Filled ball at the source (active element), filled arrowhead at the target.

notes.back: Represents that an entity plays a critical role in the creation, achievement, sustenance, or operation of a more abstract entity — e.g., a business process realizes a business service; a data object realizes a business object.
notes.extra:
Line style: dotted line

Dotted line with hollow (open) triangle pointing at the more abstract (realized) element.

notes.back: Represents that an element provides its functionality to another element — e.g., an application service serves a business process; a business interface serves a business actor.
notes.extra:
Line style: solid line

Solid line with open (line) arrowhead pointing at the element being served (the consumer). Called 'used by' in older ArchiMate versions.

notes.back: Represents the ability of behavior and active structure elements to observe or act upon passive structure elements — e.g., a business process accesses a business object.
notes.extra:
Line style: dotted line

Dotted line; arrowhead points at the passive element for write, at the accessor for read, both ends for read/write, no arrowhead for unspecified access.

notes.back: Represents that an element affects the implementation or achievement of some motivation element — e.g., a goal positively or negatively influences another goal. Strength can be annotated (e.g., +, ++, −, 0..10).
notes.extra:
Line style: dashed line

Dashed line with open arrowhead; the only relationship whose target must be a motivation element. Used mainly between motivation elements.

notes.back: Represents an unspecified relationship, or one that is not represented by another ArchiMate relationship.
notes.extra:
Line style: solid line

Plain solid line; a directed association has a half arrowhead at the target (e.g., applied-to end of a contract, source of data in a flow specification).

notes.back: Represents a temporal or causal relationship between elements — e.g., one business process triggers the next, or a business event triggers a business process.
notes.extra:
Line style: solid line

Solid line with filled arrowhead at the successor.

notes.front: In ArchiMate, what is a Flow relationship?
notes.back: Represents transfer from one element to another — of information, goods, money, or value — e.g., a flow of order data between two processes.
notes.extra:
Line style: dashed line

Dashed line with filled arrowhead; can be labeled with what is transferred.

notes.back: Represents that an element is a particular kind of another element of the same type — e.g., 'Take out travel insurance' specializes the process 'Take out insurance'.
notes.extra:
Line style: solid line

Solid line with hollow triangle pointing at the more GENERAL element. The only relationship allowed between two elements of the same type in all cases.

notes.back: A connector that joins or splits relationships of the same type. Filled circle = and (all paths); open circle = or (a choice).

notes.front: Recognise: open-circle connector splitting a triggering relationship
notes.back: An or-junction: a choice; only one (or some) of the paths is taken.

notes.front: Can one junction join a triggering and a flow relationship? Why?
notes.back: No. A junction joins relationships of the same type only; mixing types would make the meaning ambiguous.

notes.text: ArchiMate relationship strength, strongest → weakest: composition → aggregation → {{c1::assignment}} → {{c2::realization}} → {{c3::serving}} → {{c4::access}} → {{c5::influence}} → association.
notes.extra: Used by the derivation rule: a chain derives to its weakest link.

notes.front: Order the relationship groups by strength and say why this ordering matters.
notes.back: Structural (composition, aggregation, assignment, realization) are stronger than dependency (serving, access, influence, association). A derived relationship takes the weakest link in the chain.

notes.text: ArchiMate line styles: {{c1::dotted}} = realization and access; {{c2::dashed}} = flow and influence; {{c3::solid}} = all others.

notes.front: Composition vs aggregation: what is the difference?
notes.back: Composition: a part belongs to exactly one whole and cannot exist without it (filled diamond). Aggregation: a part may belong to several wholes and exists independently (open diamond).
notes.analogy: Rooms compose a house; employees are aggregated into project teams.

notes.front: A team can move between departments. Composition or aggregation from department to team, and why?
notes.back: Aggregation: the team exists independently and may belong to several wholes. Composition would tie it to one department.

notes.front: Serving vs realization: what is the difference?
notes.back: Realization: a concrete element brings an abstract one into existence (process realizes service). Serving: an element provides functionality to a consumer (service serves process).

notes.front: Triggering vs flow: what is the difference?
notes.back: Triggering: temporal/causal order (A causes or precedes B). Flow: something is transferred from A to B; no causation implied.

notes.front: Process A hands data to B, but B can start at any time. Triggering or flow?
notes.back: Flow: data is transferred, but A does not cause or order B. Use triggering only if A starts or precedes B.

notes.front: Access vs association: what is the difference?
notes.back: Access: behavior/active structure reads or writes a passive element. Association: any unspecified relationship between any concepts.

notes.front: Why use association sparingly, and when is it the right choice?
notes.back: It is the weakest, least specific relationship: it hides meaning. Use it only when no other relationship fits or the exact type is not yet known.

notes.front: ArchiMate motivation metamodel: how do stakeholder, driver, assessment, goal, outcome and requirement connect?
notes.back: Stakeholder associated with drivers; assessments analyse drivers and influence goals; outcomes, principles and requirements realize goals.
notes.extra: Requirements realize principles; a constraint is a specialization of requirement.

notes.back: The role of an individual, team, or organization (or classes thereof) that represents their interests in the effects of the architecture.
notes.extra:
Layer: Motivation

Aspect: Motivation

Examples: board, CEO (Chief Executive Officer), customer, regulator.

notes.back: An external or internal condition that motivates an organization to define its goals and implement the changes necessary to achieve them.
notes.extra:
Layer: Motivation

Aspect: Motivation

Examples: customer satisfaction, regulatory change, profitability.

notes.back: The result of an analysis of the state of affairs of the enterprise with respect to some driver.
notes.extra:
Layer: Motivation

Aspect: Motivation

Example: 'Customers complain about waiting times' — often a SWOT (Strengths, Weaknesses, Opportunities, Threats) outcome.

notes.back: A high-level statement of intent, direction, or desired end state for an organization and its stakeholders.
notes.extra:
Layer: Motivation

Aspect: Motivation

Example: 'Increase customer satisfaction by 10%'.

notes.back: An end result, effect, or consequence of a certain state of affairs.
notes.extra:
Layer: Motivation

Aspect: Motivation

Outcomes realize goals; results are tangible, possibly quantitative. Example: 'First-contact resolution rate raised to 90%'.

notes.back: A statement of intent defining a general property that applies to any system in a certain context in the architecture.
notes.extra:
Layer: Motivation

Aspect: Motivation

Broader than a requirement: normative for ALL systems in a context (e.g., 'Data is stored only in EU data centers'); realized by requirements.

notes.back: A statement of need defining a property that applies to a specific system as described by the architecture.
notes.extra:
Layer: Motivation

Aspect: Motivation

Realizes goals/principles for a SPECIFIC system.

notes.back: A limitation on aspects of the architecture, its implementation process, or its realization.
notes.extra:
Layer: Motivation

Aspect: Motivation

Specialization of requirement — restricts HOW, e.g., budget, deadline, or mandated technology.

notes.back: The knowledge or expertise present in, or the interpretation given to, a concept in a particular context.
notes.extra:
Layer: Motivation

Aspect: Motivation

Typically associated with a business object or representation.

notes.back: The relative worth, utility, or importance of a concept.
notes.extra:
Layer: Motivation

Aspect: Motivation

Often attached to services or products; can be associated with any element.

notes.front: Which relationship connects core elements to motivation elements such as requirements?
notes.back: Realization: a core element (process, component, service) realizes a requirement, and requirements realize goals, tracing the architecture back to intent.
notes.extra: Influence and association can also connect them.

notes.front: Why does a requirement realize a goal while an assessment only influences it?
notes.back: Realization: the requirement helps achieve the goal. Influence: the assessment pushes the goal positively or negatively without achieving it.

notes.front: In architecture description, what is a concern?
notes.back: An interest in a system relevant to one or more stakeholders, e.g., performance, cost, security, compliance.

notes.front: Goal vs outcome vs requirement: what is the difference?
notes.back: Goal: intended end state. Outcome: achieved, often measured result that realizes a goal. Requirement: property a specific system must have.

notes.front: Principle vs requirement: what is the difference?
notes.back: Principle: applies to all systems in a context. Requirement: applies to one specific system; requirements realize principles.

notes.front: Constraint vs requirement: what is the difference?
notes.back: Requirement: a need the system must satisfy. Constraint: a limitation on the architecture or its implementation (budget, standard, deadline) that restricts how needs can be met.

notes.front: Driver vs goal: what is the difference?
notes.back: Driver: a condition that motivates change (e.g., NIS2 regulation). Goal: the end state chosen in response (e.g., NIS2-compliant by Q4).

notes.front: Model in ArchiMate: regulator demands faster responses → aim to cut handling time 30% → new claims process.
notes.back: Stakeholder 'Regulator' — driver 'Compliance'; assessment 'Responses too slow' influences goal 'Cut handling time 30%'; requirement 'Automate intake' realizes the goal; process 'Handle claim' realizes the requirement.

notes.front: ArchiMate strategy metamodel: how do resource, capability, course of action and value stream connect?
notes.back: Resources assigned to capabilities; capabilities and resources realize courses of action; capabilities serve value streams.
notes.extra: Courses of action realize goals; core elements realize capabilities.

notes.back: An asset owned or controlled by an individual or organization.
notes.extra:
Layer: Strategy

Aspect: Structure (passive/active)

Tangible (people, machines, money) or intangible (brand, data). Square corners: structure element.

notes.back: An ability that an active structure element, such as an organization, person, or system, possesses.
notes.extra:
Layer: Strategy

Aspect: Behavior

Rounded corners: behavior element. Typically realized by people, processes, and technology in combination.

notes.back: A sequence of activities that create an overall result for a customer, stakeholder, or end user.
notes.extra:
Layer: Strategy

Aspect: Behavior

Added in ArchiMate 3.1. Stages are modeled as value streams composed/aggregated of value streams, connected by flow; capabilities serve value stream stages.

notes.back: An approach or plan for configuring some capabilities and resources of the enterprise, undertaken to achieve a goal.
notes.extra:
Layer: Strategy

Aspect: Behavior

Strategy or tactic; realized by capabilities and resources, realizes goals/outcomes.

notes.front: Resource vs capability vs course of action vs value stream: one line each?
notes.back: Resource: what you have. Capability: what you can do. Course of action: what you choose to do. Value stream: what you perform end to end for a customer.

notes.front: How does a capability differ from a business process?
notes.back: A capability is a stable ability, independent of how it is done. A process is one way of exercising it; processes, resources and services realize the capability.

notes.front: Capability-based planning: how do goal, course of action, capability and resource connect?
notes.back: Course of action realizes goal; capability realizes course of action; resource assigned to capability.

notes.front: Capability-based planning: what realizes a capability, and what does the capability serve?
notes.back: Processes and services realize the capability; the capability serves value-stream stages.

notes.front: Business Layer metamodel, active side: how do actor, role and behavior connect?
notes.back: Actor assigned to role; role assigned to business behavior (process, function or interaction).
notes.extra: Events trigger behavior; a product aggregates services, objects and a contract.

notes.front: Business Layer metamodel, external side: how do behavior, service, interface and business object connect?
notes.back: Behavior realizes a business service; the service is exposed via a business interface; behavior accesses business objects.
A business entity that is capable of performing behavior.
notes.extra:
Layer: Business

Aspect: Active Structure

A person, department, or organization — performs behavior via assigned roles.

notes.back: The responsibility for performing specific behavior, to which an actor can be assigned, or the part an actor plays in a particular action or event.
notes.extra:
Layer: Business

Aspect: Active Structure

Decouples WHO (actor) from the responsibility (role); actor —assignment→ role —assignment→ process.

notes.back: An aggregate of two or more business internal active structure elements that work together to perform collective behavior.
notes.extra:
Layer: Business

Aspect: Active Structure

Performs business interactions; often temporary.

notes.back: A point of access where a business service is made available to the environment.
notes.extra:
Layer: Business

Aspect: Active Structure (external)

A channel: phone desk, web chat, branch office. Same 'lollipop' icon as other interfaces.

notes.back: A sequence of business behaviors that achieves a specific result such as a defined set of products or business services.
notes.extra:
Layer: Business

Aspect: Behavior

Ordered ('how'); icon is an arrow. Compare business function (grouped by criteria).

notes.back: A collection of business behavior based on a chosen set of criteria (such as required business resources and/or competencies), closely aligned to an organization, but not necessarily explicitly governed by the organization.
notes.extra:
Layer: Business

Aspect: Behavior

Grouped by skills/resources ('what'), stable over time; processes typically use multiple functions.

notes.back: A unit of collective business behavior performed by (a collaboration of) two or more business roles.
notes.extra:
Layer: Business

Aspect: Behavior

Performed by a business collaboration.

notes.back: An organizational state change.
notes.extra:
Layer: Business

Aspect: Behavior

Something that happens (internally or externally) and may trigger or be triggered/thrown by behavior; instantaneous or with duration. Example: 'Claim received'.

notes.back: Explicitly defined behavior that a business role, business actor, or business collaboration exposes to its environment.
notes.extra:
Layer: Business

Aspect: Behavior (external)

External view: hides internal processes; provides value to the consumer.

notes.back: A concept used within a particular business domain.
notes.extra:
Layer: Business

Aspect: Passive Structure

Informational/conceptual, e.g., 'Invoice', 'Insurance Policy'; realized by data objects or representations.

notes.back: A formal or informal specification of an agreement between a provider and a consumer that specifies the rights and obligations associated with a product and establishes functional and non-functional parameters for interaction.
notes.extra:
Layer: Business

Aspect: Passive Structure

Specialization of business object; part of a product.

notes.back: A perceptible form of the information carried by a business object.
notes.extra:
Layer: Business

Aspect: Passive Structure

E.g., a printed bill or a PDF (Portable Document Format) form; realizes a business object.

notes.back: A coherent collection of services and/or passive structure elements, accompanied by a contract/set of agreements, which is offered as a whole to (internal or external) customers.
notes.extra:
Layer: Business

Aspect: Composite

Composite element: aggregates business/application/technology services, objects, and a contract. Example: 'Travel insurance' product.

notes.front: Business process vs business function: when do you model which?
notes.back: Process: ordered flow to a defined result, often cross-department ('Handle claim'). Function: behavior grouped by skills/resources, stable ('Finance').
notes.analogy: A function is a department of the kitchen (pastry, grill); a process is the path one order takes through them.

notes.front: Why model a business role between the actor and the process?
notes.back: It decouples who from the responsibility: actor → assigned to role → assigned to process, so reassigning people needs no change to behavior.

notes.front: Two departments perform the same business process with different people. Which elements keep one process model valid?
notes.back: Define one business process and one role; assign each department's actors to that role. The behavior is unchanged.

notes.front: Product vs business service: what is the difference?
notes.back: Business service: one unit of exposed behavior. Product: a composite of services, passive elements and a contract, offered as a whole.

notes.front: Collaboration vs interaction: what is the difference?
notes.back: Collaboration (active structure): two or more active elements working together. Interaction (behavior): the collective behavior they perform; the collaboration is assigned to it.

notes.front: Service vs interface: what is the difference?
notes.back: Service: what is offered (exposed behavior). Interface: where it is accessed (the channel/access point); assigned to the service.
notes.analogy: Service = a bank's 'transfer money'; interfaces = app, branch counter, phone line.

notes.front: A node's implementation is replaced but its technology service is unchanged. What happens to the models of consumers?
notes.back: Nothing: consumers depend on the technology service (serving), not on the node behind it. Only the realizing elements change.

notes.front: Business object vs data object vs artifact vs representation?
notes.back: Business object: domain concept ('Policy'). Data object: logical data ('Policy record'). Artifact: physical file ('policy.parquet'). Representation: human-perceptible form (printed policy).
notes.extra: Data object and representation realize the business object; artifact realizes the data object.

notes.front: ArchiMate Application Layer metamodel: how do component, function, service, interface and data object connect?
notes.back: Component assigned to application function; function realizes application service, exposed via an interface the component composes; function accesses data objects.
An encapsulation of application functionality aligned to implementation structure, which is modular and replaceable.
notes.extra:
Layer: Application

Aspect: Active Structure

A whole application or modular part of it; the UML (Unified Modeling Language) component icon with two tabs.

notes.back: An aggregate of two or more application internal active structure elements that work together to perform collective application behavior.
notes.extra:
Layer: Application

Aspect: Active Structure

E.g., front-end and back-end components jointly handling a transaction.

notes.back: A point of access where application services are made available to a user, another application component, or a node.
notes.extra:
Layer: Application

Aspect: Active Structure (external)

E.g., an API (Application Programming Interface) or a GUI (Graphical User Interface).

notes.back: Automated behavior that can be performed by an application component.
notes.extra:
Layer: Application

Aspect: Behavior

Internal behavior grouped by functionality; realizes application services.

notes.back: A unit of collective application behavior performed by (a collaboration of) two or more application components.
notes.extra:
Layer: Application

Aspect: Behavior

notes.back: A sequence of application behaviors that achieves a specific result.
notes.extra:
Layer: Application

Aspect: Behavior

Ordered automated behavior, e.g., a straight-through claims-processing flow.

notes.back: An application state change.
notes.extra:
Layer: Application

Aspect: Behavior

E.g., 'message received'; may trigger application behavior.

notes.back: An explicitly defined exposed application behavior.
notes.extra:
Layer: Application

Aspect: Behavior (external)

Serves business processes/functions or other application components.

notes.back: Data structured for automated processing.
notes.extra:
Layer: Application

Aspect: Passive Structure

Logical data; realizes business objects, realized by artifacts.

notes.front: Which two relationships mainly align the Application Layer to the Business Layer?
notes.back: Serving (application service serves business behavior) and realization (data object realizes business object; application process may realize business process).
notes.extra: Aggregation is also used across layers inside a product: a product may aggregate application and technology services and data objects.

notes.front: Which direction does a serving arrow point, and what does that mean?
notes.back: From the provider to the consumer (arrowhead at the served element): e.g. an application service serves a business process.

notes.front: Which relationships align the Technology Layer to the Application Layer?
notes.back: Serving (technology service serves components) and realization (artifact realizes component or data object). Assignment deploys artifacts on nodes.

notes.front: Can a node serve a business process directly in a view? What justifies it?
notes.back: Yes, via a derived relationship: node → artifact → component → application service → process collapses (weakest-link rule) to node serving process.

notes.front: ArchiMate Technology Layer metamodel: how do node, artifact, technology service, path and network connect?
notes.back: Node assigned to technology behavior, which realizes technology services; artifacts are assigned to (deployed on) nodes; paths connect nodes and are realized by networks.
A computational or physical resource that hosts, manipulates, or interacts with other computational or physical resources.
notes.extra:
Layer: Technology

Aspect: Active Structure

Generic infrastructure resource; devices and system software are specializations.

notes.back: A physical IT (Information Technology) resource upon which system software and artifacts may be stored or deployed for execution.
notes.extra:
Layer: Technology

Aspect: Active Structure

Specialization of node: server, router, smartphone.

notes.back: Software that provides or contributes to an environment for storing, executing, and using software or data deployed within it.
notes.extra:
Layer: Technology

Aspect: Active Structure

Specialization of node: operating system, DBMS (Database Management System), application server, container runtime.

notes.back: An aggregate of two or more technology internal active structure elements that work together to perform collective technology behavior.
notes.extra:
Layer: Technology

Aspect: Active Structure

E.g., a cluster of nodes jointly providing failover.

notes.back: A point of access where technology services offered by a node can be accessed.
notes.extra:
Layer: Technology

Aspect: Active Structure (external)

E.g., a network port, a management API (Application Programming Interface).

notes.back: A link between two or more nodes, through which these nodes can exchange data, energy, or material.
notes.extra:
Layer: Technology

Aspect: Active Structure

Logical communication link; realized by one or more networks.

notes.back: A set of structures that connects nodes for transmission, routing, and reception of data.
notes.extra:
Layer: Technology

Aspect: Active Structure

Physical communication medium, e.g., a LAN (Local Area Network); realizes paths.

notes.back: A collection of technology behavior that can be performed by a node.
notes.extra:
Layer: Technology

Aspect: Behavior

notes.back: A sequence of technology behaviors that achieves a specific result.
notes.extra:
Layer: Technology

Aspect: Behavior

E.g., an automated backup or deployment procedure.

notes.back: A unit of collective technology behavior performed by (a collaboration of) two or more nodes.
notes.extra:
Layer: Technology

Aspect: Behavior

notes.back: A technology state change.
notes.extra:
Layer: Technology

Aspect: Behavior

E.g., 'disk full', 'message arrived'.

notes.back: An explicitly defined exposed technology behavior.
notes.extra:
Layer: Technology

Aspect: Behavior (external)

E.g., messaging, storage, or processing services serving application components.

notes.back: A piece of data that is used or produced in a software development process, or by deployment and operation of an IT (Information Technology) system.
notes.extra:
Layer: Technology

Aspect: Passive Structure

E.g., a container image, WAR (Web Application Archive) file, configuration file; realizes data objects and application components; assigned to (deployed on) nodes.

notes.front: Typical deployment pattern in the ArchiMate Technology Layer?
notes.back: Artifact 'app.jar' realizes component; artifact assigned to node (or system software on a device); technology service serves the component.
One or more physical machines, tools, or instruments that can create, use, store, move, or transform materials.
notes.extra:
Layer: Physical

Aspect: Active Structure

Specialization of node; e.g., an assembly robot or a bottling machine.

notes.back: A physical structure or environment.
notes.extra:
Layer: Physical

Aspect: Active Structure

E.g., a factory, warehouse, or data center; often composes/aggregates equipment.

notes.back: A physical network used to transport materials or energy.
notes.extra:
Layer: Physical

Aspect: Active Structure

Physical counterpart of the communication network; e.g., rail network, power grid, pipeline.

notes.back: Tangible physical matter or physical elements.
notes.extra:
Layer: Physical

Aspect: Passive Structure

E.g., raw materials, fuel, paper; accessed by physical/technology behavior.

notes.front: What do physical elements add to the Technology Layer, and why can technology behavior elements describe them?
notes.back: They extend it: equipment is a specialization of node, so technology behavior elements model its behavior; material is the passive element.

notes.front: Node vs device vs system software vs equipment?
notes.back: Node: generic resource. Device: physical IT hardware. System software: execution environment. Equipment: machines working on materials. All three specialize node.

notes.front: Path vs communication network vs distribution network?
notes.back: Path: logical link between nodes. Communication network: physical data infrastructure realizing paths. Distribution network: transports materials or energy.

notes.front: Implementation & Migration metamodel: how do events, work packages, deliverables and plateaus connect?
notes.back: Implementation events trigger work packages; work packages realize deliverables; deliverables realize plateaus.

notes.front: What does an ArchiMate gap relate to, and what does it express?
notes.back: A gap is associated with two plateaus and states the difference between them.
A series of actions identified and designed to achieve specific results within specified time and resource constraints.

notes.front: How is a gap used in migration planning?
notes.back: The gap between baseline and target plateaus shows what is missing or changed; work packages are defined to close it.

notes.front: How do you show that a new application component is delivered by a project and exists in the target state?
notes.back: A deliverable realizes the component; the target plateau aggregates it; a gap is associated with the elements that differ between plateaus.

notes.front: How do you structure a transition roadmap in ArchiMate?
notes.back: Plateaus for baseline, transitions and target; a gap between consecutive plateaus; implementation events mark milestones.
notes.extra: Maps to TOGAF Baseline / Transition / Target Architectures.

notes.front: Plateau vs deliverable: what is the difference?
notes.back: Plateau: a stable state of the architecture for a period. Deliverable: a defined result of a work package; deliverables realize plateaus.
A representation of a system from the perspective of a related set of concerns.
A specification of the conventions for a kind of view: which concepts, notation and analysis to use for a set of stakeholder concerns.

notes.front: View vs viewpoint: what is the difference?
notes.back: A view is what you see (content); a viewpoint is where you look from (the template/conventions). Each view is governed by one viewpoint.
notes.analogy: Viewpoint = a map legend and scale ("road map"); view = the actual road map of your region.

notes.front: A finance director cares only about cost. How do you serve this concern without showing the whole model?
notes.back: Define or choose a viewpoint for the cost concern (selected concepts, notation) and build a view from it, hiding irrelevant detail.

notes.front: In ISO/IEC/IEEE 42010, how do stakeholders, concerns, viewpoints, views and models relate?
notes.back: Stakeholders have concerns; a viewpoint frames concerns; each view is governed by one viewpoint and is composed of models.
notes.extra: Shared by TOGAF and ArchiMate.

notes.text: ArchiMate example viewpoint categories: {{c1::Basic}} (e.g., Layered, Service Realization), {{c2::Motivation}} (e.g., Goal Realization), {{c3::Strategy}} (e.g., Capability Map), {{c4::Implementation & Migration}} (e.g., Migration).

Viewpoint purpose: {{c1::Designing}} supports architects with detailed models; {{c2::Deciding}} supports managers (cross-reference tables, landscape maps); {{c3::Informing}} builds understanding and commitment (simplified illustrations).
Viewpoint content level: {{c1::Details}} = one layer and one aspect; {{c2::Coherence}} = multiple layers or aspects; {{c3::Overview}} = multiple layers and aspects.

notes.front: What are the key steps in defining an architecture viewpoint?
notes.back: Identify stakeholders and concerns → select layers, aspects and concepts → define notation → build the view (derivation hides detail) → validate with stakeholders.

notes.text: ArchiMate's two customization mechanisms: {{c1::profiles}} (sets of typed attributes attached to concepts) and {{c2::specialization}} (new concepts as particular kinds of existing ones).

notes.front: What do you inherit and what may you change when you specialize an ArchiMate element?
notes.back: It inherits the allowed relationships of its parent. You may label it «stereotype» and change its icon or notation, as long as it stays recognisable.
notes.extra: Profiles + specialization together support domain-specific extensions and quantitative analysis (e.g., cost or performance attributes).

notes.front: When would you use a profile instead of a specialization to customize ArchiMate?
notes.back: Use a profile to add attributes (e.g. cost, owner) to existing concepts. Use a specialization to create a new kind of element (e.g. «Microservice» as a kind of application component).

notes.front: State the ArchiMate derivation rule for valid structural/dependency chains.
notes.back: A chain of structural and/or dependency relationships in the same direction can be replaced by the weakest relationship in it.
notes.analogy: A chain is only as strong as its weakest link.
notes.extra: Example: component —assignment→ function —realization→ service ⇒ component —realization→ service.

notes.front: Derivation: role R is assigned to process P; P realizes service S. What is derived between R and S?
notes.back: Realization from R to S (the weaker of assignment and realization).

notes.front: Derivation: component —assignment→ function —serving→ process. What is derived?
notes.back: Component —serving→ process: serving is weaker than any structural relationship.
Valid derivations always hold (weakest-link rule on structural/dependency chains). Potential ones may hold: they involve dynamic relationships and need modeler judgment.

notes.front: Example of a potential derivation with flow?
notes.back: Role A assigned to P1, role B to P2, flow P1 → P2 ⇒ a potential flow A → B. It need not hold in every case.

notes.front: Besides the weakest-link rule, what must a derived relationship still satisfy?
notes.back: It must be allowed between those element types by the relationship tables (Appendix B), and respect direction.

notes.front: A node serves a component, and the component serves a process. What is derived, and which rule applies?
notes.back: Node serving process: a chain of same-direction dependency relationships derives to the weakest link, here serving.
